questions.question: Examine the evolution of organized charity and social welfare under the Elizabethan Poor Laws. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Examine the evolution of organized charity and social welfare under the Elizabethan Poor Laws.
  • a. Pre-Elizabethan charity was primarily church-based, unorganized, and inconsistent.
  • b. The Elizabethan Poor Law (1601) marked the first state-regulated system of social welfare.
  • c. It categorized the poor into deserving (unable to work) and undeserving (able to work).
  • d. Parish-based administration made local authorities responsible for relief distribution.
  • e. Introduced poor rate (local tax) to fund welfare support.
  • f. Workhouses and apprenticeship programmes were created to rehabilitate able-bodied poor.
  • g. Outdoor relief offered food, money, or materials to needy families.
  • h. The law laid the foundation for state involvement in welfare, replacing charity-only models.
  • i. It established accountability and record-keeping in welfare administration.
  • j. It influenced later welfare legislation in Britain and globally, shaping modern social security systems.
  • [An] /
  • [CO4]

questions.question: Evaluate the ethical dilemmas faced in performing social work functions. / [CO4]
questions.solution_html:
• Evaluate the ethical dilemmas faced in performing social work functions.
  • a. Client confidentiality vs. duty to warn when clients pose risk to others.
  • b. Client autonomy vs. beneficence, especially when clients make harmful choices.
  • c. Dual relationships that can threaten professional boundaries.
  • d. Resource allocation dilemmas when services are limited but needs are high.
  • e. Cultural sensitivity vs. universal human rights standards in diverse contexts.
  • f. Involuntary interventions (e.g., child protection, psychiatric referrals) challenge client rights.
  • g. Truth-telling vs. protecting client emotions during sensitive discussions.
  • h. Conflicts of interest when organizational goals differ from client best interests.
  • i. Advocacy vs. neutrality when social workers must take a stand on social issues.
  • j. Use of technology and digital data raises privacy and surveillance concerns.
  • E] /

  • a. Challenges oppressive structures by mobilizing communities to assert their rights.
  • b. Raises public awareness of injustice through protests, campaigns, and media advocacy.
  • c. Influences policy and law reform, ensuring rights are protected in legal frameworks.
  • [E] /
  • [CO5]
  • d. Empowers marginalized groups to participate in decision-making.
  • e. Creates collective pressure that compels institutions to change discriminatory practices.
  • f. Acts as a watchdog, monitoring human rights violations and demanding accountability.
  • g. Strengthens civil society by building networks of activists, NGOs, and rights groups.
  • h. Promotes participatory democracy by encouraging citizen engagement.
  • i. Faces resistance from power structures, highlighting the need for strategic planning.
  • j. Ensures long-term social transformation by shifting public attitudes and promoting justice.
